costGuide.title: Volvo B4204T46 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a B4204T46 is more complex than a standard petrol engine due to the hybrid system - typically 12-16 hours at £70-£90/hr (independent). Additional time may be required for electric motor and battery system integration. Confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: (All figures , based on UK specialist quotes and marketplace observations [THIRD‑PARTY].)

What moves the price on a B4204T46 replacement is significantly more than just the engine itself. The hybrid system - including the electric motor, high-voltage cabling, battery pack (if being replaced), and the integrated starter-generator - all add complexity and cost. A used unit with documented hybrid system health, PCV service, and timing belt history commands a premium. Unlike non-hybrid T5 variants, the hybrid system's condition is as important as the engine itself. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Volvo B4204T46 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: PCV System Clogging - shared with all VEA T5 variants
items.whatHappens: The B4204T46 shares the VEA T5 petrol engine architecture with non-hybrid variants, so PCV system clogging remains a concern. Crankcase ventilation becomes blocked with sludge and carbon deposits, increasing crankcase pressure and forcing oil past piston rings and turbo seals. Symptoms include oil consumption (1 litre per 1,000 km reported in some cases), blue smoke, and possible oil leaks. The hybrid system's additional start-stop cycles may accelerate sludge formation.
items.repairVsReplace: PCV system cleaning or replacement (typically £300-£600) resolves the issue if caught early. If ignored, turbo damage (£900-£1,800) or piston ring gumming (full rebuild) may result. Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Timing Belt - interference engine, critical interval
items.whatHappens: The B4204T46 uses a timing belt, not a chain. As an interference engine, a failed belt or tensioner causes pistons to strike valves, destroying the cylinder head and often the bottom end. The hybrid system's additional torque and start-stop operation may place additional strain on the belt and tensioner over time. Interval is typically 90,000 miles or 10 years.
items.repairVsReplace: Belt failure is catastrophic - full engine replacement is almost always required. Preventative belt replacement at the correct interval is essential; many specialists recommend replacing the water pump, tensioner and VVT pulleys simultaneously. Read our full timing belt failure guide

items.title: Electric Motor / Hybrid System Integration - B4204T46-specific
items.onset: 60,000-100,000 miles (electric motor bearings), battery degradation over time
items.whatHappens: The B4204T46 is always paired with an electric motor (typically on the rear axle for AWD models, or integrated into the gearbox for FWD versions). Electric motor bearing wear, high-voltage cabling faults, and battery pack degradation are specific to the hybrid system. Symptoms include loss of electric drive, charging errors, "hybrid system service required" warnings, and reduced EV range. The battery pack degrades over time and with charge cycles.
items.repairVsReplace: Electric motor bearing replacement (£800-£2,000) is specialist work. Battery pack refurbishment or replacement (£3,000-£7,000) is expensive and often the deciding factor in whether the car is worth repairing. Many specialists recommend a full hybrid system health check before committing to any engine work. Read our full hybrid system guide

items.title: Coolant Heater / HV Heater Failure - B4204T46-specific
items.whatHappens: The B4204T46 hybrid system uses an electric coolant heater to warm the cabin and battery when the engine is off. These heaters can fail, leading to loss of cabin heating in EV mode and possible battery temperature management issues. Symptoms include cold air on electric-only driving and occasional fault codes.
items.repairVsReplace: HV heater replacement (£600-£1,200) is the fix. The heater is a hybrid-specific component not found on non-hybrid VEA engines.

failures.goodYearsLine: The B4204T46 (2018+) benefits from the latest VEA petrol engineering, including improved PCV and timing components over earlier non-hybrid units. However, the hybrid system adds significant complexity. Cars with full service history, regular battery health checks, and documented PCV/timing care are more reliable than neglected examples. Battery degradation is inevitable - factor this into ownership costs on higher-mileage cars.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B4204T46
variants.intro: The B4204T46 is a specific sub‑code within the VEA 2.0‑litre T5 Twin Engine PHEV family, introduced around 2018. It is the plug-in hybrid calibration of the T5. Here's how it compares to other common VEA petrol and hybrid codes: - B4204T23 - 254hp, 2017‑2020, non-hybrid T5, most powerful single-turbo - B4204T41 - 245‑250hp, 2014‑present, non-hybrid high-output T5 - B4204T46 - PHEV, 2018‑present, T5 Twin Engine with electric motor and battery pack - B4204T47 - Similar PHEV variant, different battery/calibration - B4204T56 / T57 - Later PHEV variants with larger battery packs - B4204T27 - 320hp T6 twin‑charged (supercharger + turbo) - completely different configuration Where the code is found: The B4204T46 sub‑code is printed on a sticker on the timing belt cover and on the V5C registration document under "Engine number". The first three characters (B42) indicate the VEA petrol family, and the final digits give the specific variant. Commonly confused codes: The B4204T46 is often mistaken for non-hybrid T5 variants (B4204T23, B4204T41) or other PHEV variants (B4204T47). They are not identical - the T46 has hybrid-specific ancillaries, a different starter-generator, and unique ECU calibration. Fitting a non-hybrid T5 into a PHEV car will not work - the hybrid system cannot communicate with a non-hybrid ECU.

relatives.description: B4204T41 / B4204T23 (non - hybrid T5): The non-hybrid VEA T5 variants that preceded the B4204T46. The B4204T41 (245‑250hp, 2014‑present) and B4204T23 (254hp, 2017‑2020) share the same block and major components but lack the electric motor, high-voltage battery, hybrid starter-generator and PHEV-specific ECU calibration. A non-hybrid T5 cannot be used to replace a B4204T46 - the hybrid system integration is fundamentally different. |

B4204T56 / B4204T57 (later PHEV variants): The later VEA PHEV calibrations that followed the B4204T46, with larger battery packs (up to 18.8 kWh) and increased electric - only range (up to 55 miles). The T56 and T57 variants are found in later-model S60, V60, XC60 and XC90 PHEVs. They share the same engine block but have revised hybrid system software and different battery configurations. Not a straight swap without matching the battery and control modules.

B4204T47 (similar PHEV variant): The B4204T47 is a close sibling - another VEA PHEV calibration with slightly different power output or emissions tuning. The T46 and T47 are similar in architecture but may differ in ECU calibration, electric motor output, or battery management software. Not interchangeable without confirming compatibility.

D4204T (2.0L D4 diesel): The diesel counterpart in the VEA family - shares the same block architecture but is fundamentally different in fuelling, compression, turbo and ancillaries. If your car is diesel, you're on the wrong page.

B4204T27 (2.0L T6, 320hp twin - charged): The high-performance T6 variant of the VEA family - supercharged and turbocharged, producing 320hp. Shares the same block but has a supercharger, different ancillaries, and a completely different induction system. Not interchangeable with the T5 PHEV; if you're looking for T6, you're on the wrong page.

relatives.code: The B4204T46 is a Volvo-only VEA PHEV powertrain, not shared with any other manufacturer. The electric motor, battery pack and hybrid control systems are Volvo-specific designs.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B4204T46 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used B4204T46 is a complex purchase - you're buying not just the engine but the integrated hybrid system. **Crucially:** insist on a full hybrid system health check, including battery capacity test, electric motor condition report, PCV service history, and timing belt replacement records. A used engine without these risks inheriting both petrol and hybrid system issues - which could cost you significantly more than a reconditioned unit in repairs. Given the hybrid system's complexity, a used engine with unknown history is a high-risk option. Used engines service

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper B4204T46 recon addresses the PCV system, timing belt, tensioner, water pump, VVT pulleys, injector seals, and includes a full hybrid system health check - including electric motor bearings, high-voltage cabling, and battery pack condition. This is the right call for any car worth over £10,000 where you plan to keep it for 2+ years. Most recon units come with a 12‑month warranty covering both the engine and hybrid components (where applicable). Reconditioned engines service

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full B4204T46 rebuild is rarely cost‑effective compared to a reconditioned exchange unit - the labour to strip, inspect and rebuild a VEA PHEV with new pistons, rings, bearings, cylinder head work, and hybrid system integration typically exceeds £6,000 before parts. Only consider a rebuild for a high-spec, low-mileage car (e.g. an XC90 T8 Inscription) where the chassis and interior are immaculate and you have a Volvo specialist with PHEV expertise. Rebuilt engines service

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement engines through our network are supplied with 12‑month warranty and can be fitted by Volvo hybrid specialists nationwide. Supply & fit service
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The B4204T46 sits in high-value PHEV cars - from £12,000 V60 T6s to £40,000+ XC90 T8s. For a sub‑£10,000 car, a reconditioned engine at £4,500-£6,500 plus potential hybrid system work may represent 60‑80% of the car's value - evaluate battery health and overall car condition carefully. For XC90 and S90 owners, the car's retained value often justifies the investment, but battery degradation should be factored into the decision. Be honest about the car's battery health, mileage and MOT history before deciding.

items.question: How much does a Volvo B4204T46 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: Reconditioned supply-only units start from £4,500, with fitted prices typically £5,300-£7,700 including labour. Used units are cheaper at £3,000-£4,500 supply-only, but carry significantly higher risk due to the hybrid system integration. The final price depends on whether the electric motor, battery pack, hybrid cabling and PCV/timing systems have been addressed. The B4204T46's PHEV complexity means replacement costs are substantially higher than non-hybrid T5 variants. Reconditioned: £4,500-£6,500 supply-only. Used: £3,000-£4,500 supply-only. Labour: 12-16 hours at £70-£90/hr (hybrid specialist rates).

items.question: What is the common failure on the B4204T46 engine?
items.answer: The B4204T46 shares the VEA T5 petrol engine's PCV system clogging and timing belt wear issues with non-hybrid variants. However, the PHEV system adds specific concerns: electric motor bearing wear, high-voltage cabling faults, battery pack degradation, and HV coolant heater failure. The hybrid system's additional complexity means that a full health check of both the petrol engine and electric components is essential. Battery degradation is inevitable over time and is often the deciding factor in whether a high-mileage PHEV is worth repairing. PCV clogging: oil consumption can exceed 1L per 1,000km. Timing belt interval: 90,000 miles or 8‑10 years - failure = full engine replacement. Battery degradation: reduced EV range, capacity loss over time. HV heater failure: loss of cabin heating in EV mode.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned B4204T46 engine?
items.answer: The B4204T46 is a complex PHEV powertrain. For a car valued under £10,000, a used unit with documented hybrid system health, battery capacity test, PCV and timing belt history (£3,000-£4,500) may be the only option - but the risk of inheriting hybrid system issues is high. For higher-value cars (£15,000+), a reconditioned unit (£4,500-£6,500) with a full hybrid system health check, 12‑month warranty covering both petrol and electric components, and all common issues addressed is almost always the better investment. Battery condition is critical - factor in replacement costs if the battery is degraded. Used: lower cost, higher risk of hybrid system issues. Reconditioned: all common failure points addressed, warranty included. For B4204T46: insist on battery health test and hybrid system report.

items.question: Can I replace a B4204T46 with a non-hybrid T5 engine?
items.answer: No. The B4204T46 is a plug-in hybrid powertrain that relies on ECU integration with the electric motor, high-voltage battery, and hybrid control module. A non-hybrid T5 (B4204T23, B4204T41, etc.) lacks the necessary hardware connections, starter-generator, and ECU calibration to operate the hybrid system. Fitting a non-hybrid engine will result in numerous fault codes, loss of electric drive, and potentially safety system warnings. Always replace with a matching B4204T46 (or a compatible later PHEV variant with confirmed ECU matching). Non-hybrid T5 not compatible with PHEV systems. Must match sub‑code (B4204T46, B4204T47, etc.). ECU and hybrid control module require matching.
bullets: Non-hybrid T5 not compatible with PHEV systems
ECU and hybrid control module require matching

items.question: How long does a B4204T46 engine and hybrid system last?
items.answer: The petrol engine itself, with proper maintenance, can achieve 150,000-200,000 miles. However, the hybrid system components have different lifespans: the electric motor typically lasts 150,000+ miles, but the high-voltage battery degrades over time - typically 8‑10 years or 100,000 miles before significant capacity loss. The hybrid system's additional complexity means that total powertrain longevity depends on both engine and battery health. Regular battery health checks, PCV service, and strict timing belt adherence are essential for maximum lifespan. Timing belt: 90,000 miles or 8‑10 years. Battery: 8‑10 years typical lifespan before significant degradation. Electric motor: durable but bearings can wear at higher mileages.

Electric motor: durable but bearings can wear at higher mileages
